entries.title: City Council raises debt threshold, setting stage for potential fourth veto from Mayor Johnson
entries.summary: <p>A defiant City Council tried Tuesday to wean Chicago off its historic addiction to debt, setting the stage for a potential fourth veto from Mayor Brandon Johnson.</p><p>By a vote of 32 to 15, the City Council agreed to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/14/city-council-finance-committee-borrowing-threshold-marty-quinn" >require future borrowing</a> to be approved by a three-fifths vote. That’s 30 votes instead of the current threshold of 26 votes.</p><p>But the Council's support in favor of the reform championed by retiring Ald. Marty Quinn (13th) fell short of the 34 votes that would be required to override a mayoral veto. That means Quinn’s political victory could be short-lived.</p><p>“The mayor does have a history of vetoing really good policy. He vetoed the hemp [ban]. He decided to choose dodgy storefronts over the safety of kids, so anything is possible,” Quinn said, acknowledging that 34 votes is “a reach.”</p><p>“The policy is solid. Having more eyes around debt is a good thing. Involving more alders in the vote total creates more attendance, which I’ve been after for the last five years."</p><p>Budget Committee Chair Jason Ervin (28th) has argued that if 26 votes is “enough to pass any and every” other piece of legislation, it makes no sense to “allow a minority of members to effectively hold everybody hostage.”</p><p>Johnson has hinted strongly at another veto, arguing that Chicagoans “need us to move with expediency” to fill potholes, trim trees and repair or rebuild Chicago bridges that are crumbling because of “negligence over decades.”</p><p>But with 40% of Chicago’s operating budget gobbled up by pension and debt payments, Quinn isn’t he only one who has targeted the city’s mountain of debt.</p><p>The Civic Committee of the Commercial Club, one of Chicago’s most influential business groups, made debt issuance a focal point of its financial recommendations to the city. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/24/civic-committee-commercial-club-of-chicago-city-hall-financial-crisis-recommendations" >In a report released last week,</a> the group recommended that city debt “only be issued to pay for capital needs” and that savings generated by debt refinancing be used “over the life of the bond term” and never for “immediate budget relief.”</p><p>The committee also recommended that the city “adopt the goal of paying down 25% of debt within five years and 50% within ten years.”</p><p> </p><p>Under Johnson's stewardship, last year the city borrowed $449.3 million to bankroll large settlements and retroactive pay raises for Chicago firefighters that City Council members had been assured would be covered by money already set aside in the city budget.</p><p>And just last month, Johnson refinanced up to $525 million in city debt to erase an $85.1 million mid-year shortfall without employee layoffs and allowed to use what’s left of federal pandemic relief funds to help close the gap, if needed.</p><p>Those are the kinds of short-term fixes that the Council's 29-member opposition coalition has ruled out in the upcoming budget debate. </p><p>“One-time money must not paper over a permanent problem. Borrowing, refinancing, reserves and asset sales have no business underwriting operations,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/28/city-council-opposition-pre-election-budget-battle-mayor-brandon-johnson" >the group wrote in a letter</a> to the mayor this week.</p><p>Even if Johnson uses his fourth veto to block the higher threshold, Quinn said he will have made his point about the danger of borrowing more money and, increasingly, structuring the repayment schedule to postpone the day of reckoning. Last year, the Council almost blocked an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/02/18/830-million-bond-issue-city-borrowing-costs-backloaded-repayment-schedule" target="_blank" >$830 million general obligation bond issue</a> that included a back-loaded repayment schedule that raised the overall price tag to $2 billion. </p><p>“When you’re pushing debt down the road or you have too much debt, it has an adverse impact on our bond rating and we’re going to have to spend more money for what we borrow,” Quinn said Tuesday.</p><p>With the mayoral election less than five months away, Ervin has accused Johnson’s City Council opposition of having political motives.</p><p>Quinn denied that his motives were political, saying the measure is the next logical step toward a truly independent City Council.</p><p>“Utilizing a three-fifths vote as opposed to a simple majority allows more voices to be heard and counted," Quinn said. "This isn’t a new concept. A three-fifths vote is required in the Illinois General Assembly on all debt-related matters. It’s a smart and solid practice that, I believe, the city should also adopt.”</p><p>Civic Federation President Joe Ferguson has countered that raising the bar for issuing new city debt “isn’t a political thing. This is math.”</p><p>According to the Civic Federation, the city’s outstanding net debt rose by 32.8%, from $22 billion to $29.2 billion, between 2014 and 2023 — an amount driven by increased O’Hare Airport debt that was retired by airline revenue.</p>

entries.title: Kankakee forfeits Lincoln-Way West win due to ineligible player, placed on probation by IHSA
entries.summary: <p>Kankakee has forfeited a win against Lincoln-Way West on Sept. 18 for using an ineligible player. The Illinois High School Association placed the Kays on probation for the rest of the season.</p><p>The Kays, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/09/27/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >ranked No. 20 in the Super 25</a>, beat Lincoln-Way West 28-14 in the game. Kankakee AD Chris Pickett did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Lincoln-Way West and Kankakee are both 4-2 after the change. </p><p>“We recognize that eligibility mistakes can and do occur, and we appreciate Kankakee High School being forthcoming in not only reporting the violation but also presenting a plan to remedy this situation from occurring again in the future," IHSA Executive Director Craig Anderson said in a statement. "The school’s football program was also placed on probation by the IHSA for the remainder of the season. Probation does not deny the school or program any IHSA privileges, but it does set the expectation that any further violations could result in more serious consequences.”</p>

entries.title: Cubs playoff roster set for opening-round series vs. Padres
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO – The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ roster for their best-of-three series against the Padres is in.</p><p>The team is carrying a dozen pitchers:</p><p>– Javier Assad</p><p>– Matthew Boyd</p><p>– Aaron Civale</p><p>– Kevin Gausman</p><p>– Clay Holmes</p><p>– Shota Imanaga</p><p>– Daniel Palencia</p><p>– David Peterson</p><p>– Colin Rea</p><p>– Ryan Rolison</p><p>– Jacob Webb</p><p>– Ryan Zeferjahn</p><p>Manager Craig Counsell said both Gausman, the righty who’s been bothered by his left shoulder since making a diving tag play last week, and Imanaga, who threw 12 pitches in an inning of work Sunday, will pitch in the series, though it’s uncertain, at this point, how they will be deployed.</p><p>Counsell’s commitment to a staff full of “out-getters” without specific roles come playoff time shows in the large number of starters and multi-inning relievers on this list. They could be asked to pitch in their more traditional roles or to be used in more non-traditional situations, the nature of playoff pitching.</p><p>Veteran lefty reliever Caleb Thielbar was not included on the roster after finishing the regular season with a 4.68 ERA and 11 home runs allowed.</p><p>Right-hander Edward Cabrera, who was acquired in a high-profile offseason trade but struggled this season with injuries and underperformance, was also absent. He was placed on the Family Medical Emergency List last week.</p><p>The Cubs put 14 position players on their initial playoff roster:</p><p>– Miguel Amaya</p><p>– Gabriel Arias</p><p>– Alex Bregman</p><p>– Michael Busch</p><p>– Michael Conforto</p><p>– Ian Happ</p><p>– Nico Hoerner</p><p>– Carson Kelly</p><p>– Pete Crow-Armstrong</p><p>– Pedro Ramirez</p><p>– Matt Shaw</p><p>– Seiya Suzuki</p><p>– Dansby Swanson</p><p>– Tyrone Taylor</p><p>The Cubs were undecided Monday whether Bregman would play third base, weighing whether it’d be too risky to expose him to further dangers in the field after he suffered multiple facial fractures when a foul ball hit his face a little over a week ago.</p><p>Bregman’s potential limitation to serving as a designated hitter figures to explain why Arias, who appeared in only seven games for the Cubs during the regular season, was included as an additional infielder.</p><p>Boyd gets the start in Game 1 on Tuesday night, a 9 p.m. Central first pitch in Southern California.</p><p>Game 2 will also start at 9 p.m. Central on Wednesday night. The start time for Game 3 on Thursday, should it be necessary, will depend on how many of the other wild-card series make it past two games.</p>

entries.title: City Council signs off on $2.5B parking meter sale — after making it a little better
entries.summary: <p>Nearly 20 years ago, then-Mayor Richard M. Daley <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/22/chicago-parking-meters-deal-stonepeak-partners-city-council-compromise-explainer" >struck a deal</a> that allowed him to avoid raising property taxes, but has come back to haunt him and Chicago ever since.</p><p>On Tuesday, the City Council took a vote that made that lopsided agreement a little less onerous for Chicago taxpayers.</p><p>The Council gave final approval to New York investment firm Stonepeak Partners’ $2.53 billion bid to acquire Chicago parking meters after Council leaders brokered a compromise to sweeten the sour deal for the city. The Council approved the deal by a 46-3 vote, with Alds. Byron Sigcho-Lopez, Jason Ervin and William Hall voting against it. </p><p>It calls for the city to receive a $75 million transfer fee at closing, 5% of net income going forward and 2% of the sale price if and when the meters are sold again before the deal ends in 2084.</p><p>The compromise, brokered without Mayor Brandon Johnson's input but with a strong assist from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/22/mayor-brandon-johnson-corporation-counsel-mary-richardson-lowry-resigns-renee-hatcher" >retiring Corporation Counsel Mary Richardson-Lowry,</a> also reduces costly compensation the city is required to pay for every space taken out of service.</p><p>Seven times a year, the city will be authorized to hold special events that take meters out of service for up to 10 hours without compensating Stonepeak. That’s up from the current threshold of six hours. Those so-called “true-up payments” cost the city nearly $174 million through 2025.</p><p>Stonepeak also announced that its subsidiary, Air Transport Services Group, reached an agreement to sell Omni Air International, an airline that has provided long-haul deportation flights for the Department of Homeland Security during President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign. And it has agreed to explore creating entire nonmetered city blocks as “potential electric vehicle charging stations with charging revenues shared with the city.” </p><p>Tuesday’s vote ends months of controversy that only exacerbated the tension and distrust between Johnson and the Council.</p><p>When private investors from as far away as Abu Dhabi wanted out after recouping their initial $1.15 billion investment twofold with 57 years to go on the deal, Johnson entered the competition without consulting the Council.</p><p>The mayor submitted four bids to take back the meters, topping out with a $3.2 billion bid that turned out to be hundreds of millions of dollars higher than the competition.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> Pat Dowell (3rd) chats with a reporter before the start of a Chicago City Council meeting at City Hall, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b2d6f8e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6850x3844+0+362/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa8%2F7d%2F6c460f144df5b2ee5301f4defe29%2Fcouncil-260930-02.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a8706e1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6850x3844+0+362/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa8%2F7d%2F6c460f144df5b2ee5301f4defe29%2Fcouncil-260930-02.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b2d6f8e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6850x3844+0+362/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa8%2F7d%2F6c460f144df5b2ee5301f4defe29%2Fcouncil-260930-02.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ald. Pat Dowell chats with a reporter before the start of Tuesday’s City Council meeting, where she and other City Council members approved the transfer of ownership of the city’s parking meters to Stonepeak Partners, a New York investment firm. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>This time, it was Johnson who was kept in the dark. Richardson-Lowry helped, but kept the negotiations in confidence and maintained a firewall between the Council and the mayor's office. Johnson was briefed only after the deal was done.</p><p>The Council's five-member negotiating team initially pegged the benefits at $376.2 million over the life of he deal. Downtown Ald. Bill Conway (34th), an investment banker, has called that number inflated — after Stonepeak deducts interest expenses and adds the potential for depreciation.</p><p>But almost anything would be better than the shortsighted deal Daley struck in 2008.</p><p>The $75 million up-front transfer fee will be used to chip away at the city’s $36 billion pile of unfunded pension liabilities.</p><p>Waguespack was one of only five alderpersons to vote against the original parking meter deal. He went into the latest negotiation believing the deal was “ironclad” and came out with changes he never thought were possible.</p><p>“When you go to buy a car, do you get the price that you want? No. The dealer says one thing. You say another and, at some point, you reach the middle point. And that’s what happened here,” said Waguespack. “Yes, we were given a bad deal in 2008. We tried to break it open and this is what we got: Five percent over the next 58 years.”</p><p></p><p> Ervin, alderperson of the 28th Ward favored his own eleventh-hour plan to to create a public infrastructure trust to take back the parking meters. He likened Tuesday’s roll call to the lightning-fast vote that sanctioned Daley’s decision to lease Chicago parking meters for 75 years — and forfeit decades of recurring parking meter revenues — tying the city's hands for decades.</p><p>"Every time we tried to close a street,” Chicago Parking Meters LLC said, “ 'Screw you. Pay me.’ And here we are again getting screwed,” Ervin said. “I still stand on the premise that we should take our streets back.”</p><p>In casting one of the three no votes Tuesday, Ervin said that the “irony is that some of the same things” that were said during that 2008 debate are being said now. Then and now, Ervin said, the city’s precarious financial condition was used as a reason to approve the deal.</p><p>“We chose to cower down and sell out for $75 million,” Ervin said. “History will judge us poorly.”</p><p></p><p>Hall, who voted against the deal, said African Americans have been left out of the $17 million in professional services contracts tied to Stonepeak’s acquisition of Chicago parking meters. “This is not the city we all were dreaming of,” Hall said. If the city is 27% Black, African American contractors should be “27% in the deal.” </p><p> Chicago Parking Meters LLC, a consortium that includes Morgan Stanley, Allianz Capital Partners and the Sovereign Wealth Fund of Abu Dhabi, had threatened to take legal action against the city if the sale to Stonepeak was not approved.</p><p>That was apparently enough to convince City Council members who wanted nothing to do with the parking meter deal to cast a vote they hope won’t come back to haunt the city like it did with Daley, who compounded the problem by spending the $1.15 billion in proceeds while pension funds sunk deeper into a hole.</p>

entries.title: Even with QB Caleb Williams potentially returning, NFL moves Bears-Packers Week 5 game to noon kickoff
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>-Packers rivalry tends to be one of the NFL's biggest draws, but the league and Fox opted to move the Week 5 matchup out of the late-afternoon national window. The teams now will kick off at 12 p.m. at Lambeau Field after their game was flexed out in favor of Seahawks-49ers.</p><p>The Packers announced the change Tuesday.</p><p>Not only is that typically a coveted matchup for television, but it could be Bears quarterback Caleb Williams' return. Williams has been out since suffering a significant hamstring injury and is projected to be coming back around that game.</p><p>In the meantime, the Bears host the Jets on Sunday at 12 p.m. after upending the Eagles 27-7 on Monday night.</p><p>With Williams out all week and backup quarterback Tyson Bagent in the concussion protocol for most of it, the Bears started third-stringer Case Keenum. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/28/bears-inactives-vs-eagles-k-cairo-santos-cb-tyrique-stevenson-good-to-go" >He completed 24 of 34 passes for 247 yards and two touchdowns for a 110.8 passer rating</a> and rushed for a touchdown. The Bears have not named a starter for Sunday.</p>

entries.title: Chicago cop charged with punching teenage girl during confrontation shown in viral video
entries.summary: <p>An embattled Chicago police sergeant was charged with punching a 17-year-old girl as she filmed a now-viral video that showed the cop threatening a group of kids this summer on the Southwest Side.</p><p>Jeremy Sikorski, 45, of Garfield Ridge, faces felony counts of aggravated battery in relation to the alleged attack Aug. 9 in the 5100 block of South Merrimac Avenue, according to Cook County court records. Sikorski turned himself over to police last week.</p><p>Sikorski and his family were attending a barbecue when Sikorski and two other men approached a group of teenagers in an alley, prosecutors said in a court filing. Prosecutors said the video shows Sikorski berating one of the teens about “picking on” other kids, apparently referencing an earlier fracas at a park that involved at least one of Sikorski’s children.</p><p>Sikorski then approached the teenage boy, first threatening to slap him and then warning that he would “knock your f------ a-- out” while raising a fist, prosecutors said, referencing the video. Sikorski also allegedly threatened to beat up the teen’s parents and menaced another person.</p><p>After Sikorski started to walk away, he turned back and punched the 17-year-old girl in her head, prosecutors said. Her phone fell to the ground and she was heard “sobbing in pain.”</p><p>Days later, she was diagnosed with a concussion, officials said. Prosecutors said she and five other people identified Sikorski as the assailant from a photo lineup.</p><p>Video of the incident was posted by CWB Chicago, a blog focused on crime and public safety issues.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">We have been informed that the man in this video is a Chicago police sergeant. <br><br>The name we have been given matches a known CPD sergeant, but we have not confirmed the identity, so we're withholding that info for now.<br><br>Details coming... <a href="https://t.co/tSkUgS1Svr">pic.twitter.com/tSkUgS1Svr</a></p>— CWBChicago (@CWBChicago) <a href="https://x.com/CWBChicago/status/2086920780172960196?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 10, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Sikorski’s attorney didn’t respond to a request for comment. An attorney for the girl’s family declined to comment.</p><p>The alleged attack was apparently spurred by an earlier altercation between the teenagers Sikorski confronted and a group of younger teens, described by prosecutors as the children of Sikorski and the host of the barbecue.</p><p>One of the older kids ultimately kicked one of the younger teens in the stomach, prosecutors said.</p><p>Sikorski later confronted the older teens in the alley of their home and asked if they were bullying the younger children, leading up to the attack, prosecutors said.</p><p>When police responded to a call of a battery, the mother of one of the older children told them the younger kids were the instigators of the conflict, prosecutors said.</p><p>Sikorski was stripped of his police powers two days later, police said. The Civilian Office of Police Accountability has opened an administrative investigation into the incident.</p><p>Sikorski surrendered at the Central District Sept. 22 to face charges, according to his arrest report. Prosecutors’ petition to have him held at Cook County Jail was denied during his first court hearing Sept. 23.</p><p><i>Contributing: Rosemary Sobol</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/21/chicago-police-cpd-vecchio-snelling" target="_blank" >Chicago cop with most misconduct complaints now charged with attacking woman as he faces firing</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/25/chicago-police-alberto-rodriguez-crime" target="_blank" >Chicago cop with UFC aspirations faces firing over alleged sexual assaults of girlfriend</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2026/06/03/david-ross-larry-snelling-chicago-police-cpd-copa" target="_blank" >Chicago cop faces firing after passing test to join horseback unit while sidelined with ‘unbearable’ injury</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: White Sox finalize 26-man roster for Wild Card series in Houston
entries.summary: <p>HOUSTON – Ahead of Game 1 of their Wild Card series against the Astros, the White Sox released their 26-man roster for this round of the postseason.</p><p>While manager Will Venable loves to mix-and-match with different pieces, the actual roster contains few surprises. With a short, best-of-three series, the Sox went with 12 pitchers, allowing them to carry a full complement of platoon outfielders of either handedness.</p><h3>Right-handed pitchers</h3><p><b>Huáscar Brazobán, Sean Burke, Erick Fedde, Jordan Hicks, Davis Martin, David Sandlin and Grant Taylor</b></p><p>Though Venable said there will be no “bulk” pitcher used in Game 1, he did indicate that plenty of arms used as starters throughout the regular season could see action in short stints. In contrast, Sean Burke threw a traditional pre-start bullpen on Monday, as did Astros Game 2 starter Hunter Brown, so a more typical matchup of each team’s best rotation piece could take place on Wednesday.</p><p>The most notable exclusion here is middle reliever Trevor Richards, who logged 78 ⅔ IP in just five months on the team, but also threw 3 ⅓ innings in a save just on Sunday. Brazoban made the cut despite a rough early stint with the Sox after being acquired at the trade deadline, but Venable recently endorsed how he’s looked since returning from a left lat strain.</p><p>“He's working himself in a spot where there's that trust,” Venable said. “ The changeup was really good the last couple of outings. There was a 98, 99 in there with the sinker and four-seamer.”</p><p>The Sox haven’t commented yet on how they’ll use Sandlin in the postseason, but it’s clear his form while throwing six innings of one-run ball to help clinch a playoff spot in Kansas City opened some eyes.</p><p>“We had a big talk after the Kansas City start, and obviously conversations leading up to that,” pitching coach Zach Bove told the Sun-Times. “I told him [about] the progress [he’s] shown in that start compared to maybe one of the first starts of the year, specifically landing offspeed in the zone.”</p><h3>Left-handed pitchers</h3><p><b>Bryan Hudson, Anthony Kay, Sean Newcomb, Noah Schultz and Hagen Smith</b></p><p>Smith isn’t so much starting on Tuesday as he is opening up a bullpen game, and no one in this group of pitchers are likely to make a traditional start; certainly not in this round. Kay threw five innings on Sunday, but has been getting prepared for a relief role for a couple weeks now.</p><p>“They asked if I was willing to do it, and I said ‘Yeah,’” Kay said. “At this point you know you’ve got to be willing to do anything for the team, and if that's what it takes, that's what it takes.”</p><h3>Catchers</h3><p><b>Jake Rogers and Kyle Teel</b></p><p>Rogers is back on the roster after missing the final games of the season on paternity leave, but Teel should start every game.</p><h3>Infielders</h3><p><b>Luisangel Acuña, Chase Meidroth, Colson Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Miguel Vargas</b></p><p>Even with Montgomery’s protracted offensive struggles, the Sox infield is fairly static and Acuna’s biggest chance for impact is as a late-game pinch-runner. Chase Meidroth’s sore left hamstring kept him out against the Rockies, shifting Sam Antonacci to start at second base. Venable said Meidroth should play in the Wild Card series, though he is not quite 100% recovered.</p><h3>Outfielders</h3><p><b>Sam Antonacci, Andrew Benintendi, Brenton Doyle, Randal Grichuk, Braden Montgomery, Tristan Peters and Tommy Pham.</b></p><p>White Sox outfielders operate almost like hockey players, shifting lines depending on the handedness of the opposing pitcher. Switch-hitter Braden Montgomery might ease this behavior in future years, but he’s produced better results left-handed and could be pinch-hit for against southpaws.</p><p>With the Astros throwing a bullpen game on Tuesday, and light on reliable left-handed options with reliever Steven Okert out due to injury, when and where Venable is enticed to deploy options like Grichuk and Pham before the arrival of closer Josh Hader into the game, will be a focus.</p>

entries.title: University of Chicago theoretical physicist honored as MacArthur Fellow
entries.summary: <p>When Vincenzo Vitelli fielded a call from an unknown number a few weeks ago, he exhibited extreme skepticism, believing it was a fraud or perhaps a joke orchestrated by a pal.</p><p>Vitelli, 48, a theoretical physicist and tenured professor at the University of Chicago, deals in mind-bending ideas every day, but the notion that he'd just won a MacArthur Fellowship and the $800,000 of no-strings-attached money that comes with it seemed beyond the pale. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.macfound.org/programs/awards/fellows/" target="_blank" >2026 Fellows</a> were announced by the foundation Tuesday. </p><p>"It took the people speaking on the other side of the phone quite a few minutes to convince me this was not a joke," he said.</p><p>The fellowship is an honor that is "intended to encourage people of outstanding talent to pursue their own creative, intellectual, and professional inclinations," according to the Chicago-based John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation.</p><p>Vitelli's <a class="Link" href="https://home.uchicago.edu/~vitelli/" target="_blank" >work centers on understanding the behavior</a> of information-processing agents — including humans, bots, cells and even individual molecules, which all possess the capacity for adaptive, intelligent behavior. </p><p>"Our research centers on a fundamental question: What laws govern complex systems composed of many such agents? What happens when you put them together and they start interacting? What is the emergent behavior? Can you describe them as if it was a material?"</p><p>Vitelli, who grew up in the historic town of Matera in southern Italy, said he'd like to use the fellowship money, which is paid out in equal quarterly installments over five years, to allow him to focus more on work.</p><p>"I'd like to use it to get even more freedom [on] the personal level, to intensify my push towards studying a less conventional form of physics," said Vitelli, who leads a team of about a dozen researchers. </p><p>A significant part of his work is simply inventing concepts.</p><p>"In part, my work is to imagine new materials and potentially even come up with ideas that change the notion of what a material actually is, blurring the lines of what people call materials, what people call machines, perhaps even what people call brains."</p><p>Vitelli says his mind can shift into imagination mode during his daily e-bike commute from his South Loop home to the University of Chicago's Hyde Park campus, at a concert or while taking in a play at one of Chicago's many theaters, or at home with his wife and 5-month-old son.</p><p>"It is something that can be somewhat irritating to the people around you who may observe lapses of attention on your part because your mind is flying somewhere else," he said.</p><p>Vitelli's concepts have undergone laboratory testing, but the research is still at the level of theoretical and has not resulted in any new technology or patents, he said.</p><p>When asked if he sometimes tells people he's an insurance salesman so he doesn't have to try explaining complex theories to laymen — like newspaper reporters — Vitelli said the opposite is more often true.</p><p>"Usually, if you say you're a theoretical physicist, you can achieve the same results more rapidly," he said with a laugh.</p><p>Vitelli has been a tenured physics professor at the University of Chicago since 2017. He earned his Ph.D. from Harvard University and came to Chicago from the Netherlands, where he worked as a professor at Leiden University.</p><p>"Chicago is a very vibrant city," he said. "I'm coming to appreciate it more and more."</p>
